Hello you,

Were you also raised to be humble, taught to focus on doing great work and opportunities will come? - Yea, me too.

But, unfortunately, this doesn't work anymore.

In 2026, you have to talk about yourself, your work, its impact. But it's cringy. I know. It's cringy. It's like listening to your own voice. Watching yourself in a video. It's unsettling. I felt the same. I still do. Even after posting over 800 videos with my face in them.

But here is thing, this cringe is what is holding you back. You are not visible and missing out on opportunities you didn't even know existed. What helped me was the shifting the mindset - to think of myself as a brand, a company, a service provider. Not a person. And suddenly, I could talk about myself all day long. Because I wasn't bragging about me. I was sharing something I believe in.

This one shift led to winning the Lise Meitner Medal. Working with Nobel Laureates. Supporting a prestigious €8 million European project. Real opportunities I didn't even know were possible. And deep down you know you need to be more visible. You know you should talk about yourself more often in order to advance in your career.

Every time you want to post on LinkedIn or introduce yourself at a conference, you shrink yourself. This stops on February 10th. 

A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

If you're ready to stop getting in your own way then join my Personal Branding Workshop on February 10th.

In two hours you'll build:

✓ A clear framework for your career goals (the real stuff, not wishful thinking)

✓ Your personal brand statement, ready to use everywhere

✓ Your platform strategy that actually fits your career

✓ Your AI-toolkit to do the heavy lifting

✓ An action plan you can start in 48 hours

€249 (+VAT) | February 10, 10am–12pm CET
Register now

Mary Jialu Chen, EPFL

Hortense Le Ferrand, Nanyang Technological University

"Pranoti is easy to work with, clear, engaging, and very knowledgeable. I wholeheartedly recommend her trainings."
Alex Ramadan, University of Sheffield

Two hours. Real strategy. The kind of stuff you'll use for the rest of your career.🧡

Looking forward to seeing you there.

Cheers,
Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar

How to make your elevator pitch "stick"

Your elevator pitch = Your personal branding statement. 
These are one or two sentences or maximum three sentences, which explain who you are what problem you are solving, and what is the impact of your effort. This is module 3 in my Personal Branding workshops.

A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

Module 1 - Career goals framework where you set clear, actionable, ambitious career goals.

Module 2 - Audience mapping where you write down who exactly has the power to help you reach your career goals. 

Module 3 - Personal branding statement where you get a clear formula to create your elevator pitch.

Why is it important to draft your personal branding statement?
Because the way you would introduce yourself to your collaborator would be different from how you introduce yourself to your department head or how you would introduce yourself to a peer that you met at a conference. A lot of scientists miss out on this because when they end up in a situation where they have to introduce themselves, especially in real life, they're like, oh yeah..., I'm a PhD student or Oh, I'm a postdoc.... and I'm working on this. 

You have to remember that the person you're speaking with has their own things. They have their own show going on in their own mind, so you need to be very clear as to - Who you are, what problem you're working on, and how does it impact either the society or the community or whichever group that you're solving this problem for.
Register for Personal Branding Workshop - Feb 10th

This is what I told scientists at the DTU - Denmark Technical University 🇩🇰: You should be extremely comfortable when you are introducing yourself with your personal branding statement. The goal here is to make sure you do not fumble. But how to do this? Three very simple steps:

  1. Create your branding statement in your head, think about it. 
  2. Write it down on a piece of paper with a pen. You can write it on your phone but I highly recommend the good old pen & paper.
  3. Say it out loud, to yourself. Or maybe record a voice memo of you saying it out loud. Say it in front of people you trust. You will be surprised by the encouraging response from your people 🧡

This is a sneak peek into my personal branding workshop and there's lots more I cover in our 2 hours together. If you want to join my workshop then now is the time to book your spot. Next workshop is less than 14 days away.

Why? Because your email bots have been hiding my emails from you.

"How often should I post?"

I get this question in every training. My response surprises the room because they have been told to post 3-5 times per week.

But the thing is, the algorithm doesn't care about your posting streak. It cares about whether your post is adding value to the people who read it.

A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

Here's what I've learnt:
1) Strategy over frequency - A thoughtfully crafted post every two weeks will outperform daily content that doesn't resonate.

2) Clarity over consistency - Know exactly who you're writing for and what problem you're solving for them. Group leaders transitioning from individual contributor to strategic leader need different content than early-career researchers. Specificity creates connection. Randomness creates noise.

3) Insight over activity - What shifts thinking? What validates a challenge they're facing? What offers genuine value? These questions matter far more than maintaining a calendar.

If you have a lot to say but hesitating to show up on LinkedIn then join my Personal Branding Workshop on February 10th.

Hellooo!

How are you doing? I'm not trying tobe polite. I really want to know. How ARE you doing - What's bothering you today at this very moment? Maybe I can help you.

I'll go first. I've been enjoying writing blogposts. This is a great way for me to structure my thoughts, pause and reflect. So far so good. Idea to writing is the part I love. 🧡

The part I don't love? Everything that comes after the writing.

A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

But here's what comes after the writing - The formatting in WordPress. The meta descriptions. The focus keywords. The SEO title. The design elements. The interlinking. You know, the operational stuff that turns a finished draft into a published post.

Text is one of the oldest forms of communication.
Science communication included.

I've been writing perspectives on The Science Talk for the past year, and here's what it's given me: stronger SEO, a growing portfolio of thought leadership pieces, and a consistent way to share my perspectives with the community. Writing blog posts has become one of my favourite parts of the work.

As a solopreneur, I can't just stop at the blog post. There's still the podcast to edit, the email to write, the video to record. So optimising this workflow has been on my mind for months.

I finally did it.

Here's my workflow now: I have the idea. I write my draft in Google Docs or Notes. I fine-tune it with Claude. Claude creates the HTML. And now — because I connected Claude Desktop to my self-hosted WordPress site through an MCP server — Claude also posts it directly to WordPress as a draft.

The creative work stays with me. The operational work? Claude handles it.

That's 1–2 hours saved every week. As a solopreneur, I'll take every hour I can get. 💪

If you want to connect your own WordPress site to Claude and optimise your workflow from idea to published post, I wrote the full step-by-step guide with every gotcha I hit along the way.

_html:
working together just like when we were kids

Hello helloooo,

Sooo I've been thinking about what makes scientists happy.
And collaboration keeps coming up as the favourite aspect of being a scientist. Bringing different skills and resources together to tackle ambitious research problems brings back our childhood memories when we used to play together. It's even better when this collaboration is well funded for longer periods of time, say 6 years.

This is exactly what ERC Synergy Grant are for. ERC is European Research Council and it gives grants up to €10 million (additional €4 million when justified) for 6 years to a team of scientists. Two to four principle investigators (PI) coming together and working towards a shared vision. It's awesome!

Until it's time to communicate the shared vision and research results. That's when things start falling apart. Because each PI and their host institution have their own preference and agenda. This leads to confusion, mixed messaging and uncoordinated posts. Almost always, the responsibility falls on the shoulders of the coordinator who is already overwhelmed with project work, teaching and other tasks.﻿

What's the solution here?

﻿Plan and allocate outreach budget when you are writing your grant proposal. This is the only way you are able to focus entirely on the research aspects of your project. For grants like ERC Synergy, which run for 6 years and have millions at stake, your outreach has to compliment your scientific excellence. Your deserve better than some last minute, scrappy and uncoordinated LinkedIn posts. Because at the end of the day, when you're working on something super awesome, you should tell your community about it. 😉

☝️this is valid for all kinds of research grants, not only ERC Synergy. 😉

I would love to help you with outreach aspects of your grant proposal.
I'm opening a few 20-min slots where I'll audit your research proposal for free.

Reply to this email if you want to book a 20-min-audit with me. 🧡

Cheers,
Pranoti

emails.preheader: It's in almost every proposal. Here's how to use it.

_html:
It's in almost every proposal. Here's how to use it.

﻿Hello hellooo!

Can I tell you about something that almost every scientist misses when writing a funding proposal?

It's not the science. It's not the methodology. It's not even the impact section (though yes, that too).

It's the budget where you are actually allowed to invest in yourself.

Most proposals have a section for project management, coordination, or career development activities. It goes by different names depending on the funding scheme, but it is almost always there. And almost always, scientists either leave it vague, fill it with generic descriptions, or don't use it at all.

Here's what you could put there instead: leadership training. Mentorship. One-on-one coaching. Skills workshops that are directly relevant to executing the project you are proposing.

And yes — AI literacy training counts.

Think about it this way. Your host institution will offer general training. It has to — those sessions are designed for everyone in the department, across all levels, across all disciplines. That is their job. But it is your job to invest in the specific skills that will make you a better researcher and a better PI on this project.

The funding is there. You just have to plan it in.

There is also something else happening when you do this well. A proposal that budgets thoughtfully for professional development sends a signal to reviewers: this person is thinking beyond the next three years. They understand that executing ambitious research requires building a capable, well-supported team — and that starts with the PI.

That is the kind of long-term thinking that evaluators notice.

The key is how you phrase it. "Career development" that reads as a perk will not land well. Career development that is clearly tied to project delivery — that is a completely different conversation. And that is exactly where I can help.

Keep this in mind when you are writing your next grant proposal. Share this email with your science besties.

Cheers,
Pranoti

﻿PS: If, apart from my detailed emails and helpful resources, you also some SciComm training and proposal writing support, I think you'll be happy about:

  1. Personal branding in the age of AI - 24th March, 9:30 - 12:30. Save your spot. 🧡

  3. My new service "SciComm Support for Proposal Writing" is live. 🥳

A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

Hello hellooo!

If you're working on a large consortium proposal, here's a question worth asking early: when should you bring in a science communication expert?

Most teams think about it after the grant is awarded. But by then, you've already locked in your budget.

The sweet spot is the budgeting stage — when you're adding numbers to the work packages and budget tables.

By this point, you've done the hard thinking:
✅ Your scientific concept is solid
✅ Your consortium is formed
✅ You know the shape and scale of the project

You have everything you need to make a well-informed decision about your communication work package.

This is where I can help. I work with you to shape the communication parts of your project management work package so they fit your project's actual scope — not a generic placeholder that gets cut later.

With the right budget secured from the start, your team can communicate your research and build your visibility from day one.

Speaking of which — if you're currently preparing your ERC Synergy 2027 proposal, I'm running a guidance session for exactly this. Details below!

Cheers,
Pranoti

    ➡️ ERC Advanced Grant — European Research Council (ERC) 🇪🇺 Budget: €2.5M Deadline: 27 August 2026 Best for: senior researchers with a strong independent track record looking to pursue high-risk, high-gain science.

_html:
Your proposal will be read by humans, not robots.
View in browser 

Hello hellooo!

You've probably seen of "AI guidance for scientists" but have you heard of the "AI guidance for grant proposal evaluators"?!

The European Research Council, the largest European funding agency with € 17 billion budget, has FINALLY released "The use of AI in grant proposal evaluation" guidelines for ERC panel members and remote reviewers.

TL;DR - Your proposals will be read by humans. AI use in the review process is extremely limited — essentially, reviewers can use it to improve the clarity of their written feedback. That's it.

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I'm the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    Here's the summary of the do's & don'ts for you:

    ✅ Language and grammar polishing, provided no proposal content is shared with the AI tool, and the reviewer's own arguments and judgement drive the content entirely.
    ✅ Searching for general information on a proposal's topic using AI tools (as long as the proposal itself isn't uploaded).
    ❌ Using AI to summarise a proposal, even on a local server. Understanding the proposal in full is a core reviewer task — it cannot be delegated.
    ❌ Using AI to assess scientific merit or novelty, regardless of data privacy settings. Forming scientific judgement is a human responsibility.
    ❌ Generating a draft review, even if the reviewer edits it afterwards. Drafting involves evaluative judgement — that's the line.
    ❌ Asking AI to check whether a review is "missing important points." Determining what matters in a review is itself part of the evaluator's job.
    ❌ Uploading any part of a proposal to an online tool — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini — regardless of intent. This breaches confidentiality and data protection rules.


    Why this matters for you

    Your proposal will be read by a human. A human who has now been formally reminded that they are responsible for their own assessment — fully, independently, and from the page alone.

    That raises the bar on clarity. A panel member working without AI assistance needs to grasp your research vision quickly and independently. The science has to land on its own terms. Clear, precise scientific communication is not a nice-to-have. It is what makes your proposal reviewable.

    These guidelines will evolve. But having formal, published guidance for evaluators — not just applicants — is a meaningful step forward for transparency in the funding process.

    Speaking of which — do you actually know which AI tools you're allowed to use at work, and for what? It's worth checking with your IT department or a colleague who's looked into this. And if you can't find the answers then it's about time to raise a red flag to your executive team.

    Cheers,
    Pranoti

      PS: If, apart from my email, you also like some proposal writing support, I think you'll be happy about:

      1. SciComm Support at Proposal Writing Stage where I work with principal investigators who want professional science communication that matches the ambition and budget of their grant proposal. More details are on my website.
      2. ERC Synergy Guidance — 14th April, 14:00. I'll share some of my secrets about fleshing out a winning outreach work package in your proposal. Save your spot!
      3. Some of my recent posts👇

      NotebookLM Cinematic Video Overviews: What’s new and is it worth it?

      Google just upgraded NotebookLM's video feature. Cinematic Video Overviews use Gemini, Imagen, and Veo to generate animated explainer videos from your sources — no blank canvas needed. Here's what changed and what still needs work.

      Read more

      ERC Guidelines on AI in Grant Proposal Evaluation: What Reviewers (and Applicants) Need to Know

      The ERC has published official guidelines on AI use in grant evaluation. Here's what reviewers must follow—and what it means for how you write your proposal.

      Read more

      16 European Research Funding Calls Open in 2026

      16 open European research funding calls in 2026 — ERC, EIC, NWO, UKRI, NNF, and Villum Fonden. Deadlines, budgets, and eligibility at a glance.

      Read more

Hellooo!

Today I want to share something really important with you.

Since February 2025, AI literacy in European research institutes stopped being a nice-to-have. It became law. The supervision and enforcement rules apply from 3 August 2026 onwards.

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I'm the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    What is article 4?

    Article 4 of the EU AI Act requires every organisation that builds or uses AI systems to ensure their staff have a sufficient level of AI literacy. That's not a recommendation or a best-practice guideline — it's an enforceable obligation, and it applies to essentially every research institute on the continent.

    Most researchers I speak to are vaguely aware of this. Far fewer know what to actually do about it.

    The tricky part for research institutes? You're sitting at a dual compliance point. If your team is developing an ML model, you're an AI provider. If your grants office is using an LLM to draft funding reports, you're an AI deployer. Article 4 obligations come at you from both directions.

    Add to that the fact that a particle physicist using ML for data analysis has completely different literacy needs from an administrator using a document assistant — and one-size-fits-all training won't cut it.

    So what does compliance actually look like?

    Three practical steps:

    Map your AI use first. Before any training, you need to know which AI tools are in use, by whom, and in what context. Many institutes find this picture is broader than expected — tools adopted quietly at team level, long before any central strategy was in place.

    Differentiate by role. A tiered approach works best: foundational awareness for all staff, plus role-specific competence training for those using AI directly in their work.

    Document and iterate. The AI landscape changes faster than any training programme. What matters for compliance is an active, documented approach that gets reviewed and updated. The European Commission's Living Repository of AI Literacy Practices is specifically designed to help with this.

    The good news: compliance doesn't require perfection. It requires intention, documentation, and progress.

    I wrote up the full breakdown — including what the Apply AI Strategy adds to this picture and what institutions like CERN, Helmholtz, and EMBL are doing — in this post.

    If you're thinking through what AI integration looks like for your own work or institution, the European AI Compliance Hub is a good place to start.

    Cheers,
    Pranoti Kshirsagar
    Founder, The Science Talk

Hellooo!

For the past two years I've been actively helping scientists with grants and fundraising. My clients, who are almost always active scientists, often struggle with articulating the impact of their research when writing research proposals. Because when you are deep in the process of drafting a research proposal, it’s easy to focus solely on the science. BUT the approach required for a successful application varies significantly depending on the funding agency. Whether you are targeting the ERC, NWO, or UKRI, understanding these nuances is critical for success.

This is exactly why a "copy-paste" approach to sections like impact and communication simply doesn't work.

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I'm the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    Same Goal, Different Approaches

    The requirements for different funding bodies are distinct, and as a scientist, these are differences you cannot afford to overlook:

    • Horizon Europe & ERC: While communication may not be a mandatory, explicitly mentioned section in every ERC proposal, you are being evaluated as a Principal Investigator. Here, your goal is to showcase yourself as a rising or established academic leader.
    • NWO (Netherlands): For talent programs and open competitions, the impact section is vital—often carrying as much as 25% of the total weighting. This requires a dedicated, robust strategy.
    • UKRI (United Kingdom): Impact isn't just a checkbox; it needs to be expertly woven into the very fabric of your proposal to demonstrate the broader value of your work.

    To help you navigate these differences, I have written a comprehensive summary blog post. It breaks down the specific requirements for various agencies and offers actionable advice on how to tailor your outreach and impact strategies to meet their unique expectations.

    Understanding that different grant applications need different approaches is the first step toward a winning proposal. I hope this free resource helps you sharpen your next submission!

Hello helllooo,

The EU AI Act’s transparency obligations under Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026 — and if you publish AI-generated content professionally, you have specific disclosure duties that go well beyond adding a footnote to your terms and conditions.

For the past two years I've been evaluating different AI tools and I just winged it when it came to disclosures. And so, honestly, I'm very happy to see these guidelines which will soon be regulations.

Before we move on...

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I'm the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    What's in scope: AI-generated or manipulated text published on matters of public interest (research, health, policy, environment, science). This includes blog posts, social media, video scripts, and podcast show notes.

    Where disclosures must appear: At the start of your content — before the first paragraph, at the top of captions, or as an on-screen overlay. End-of-post disclaimers and terms-and-conditions links don't meet the standard.

    What qualifies as editorial review: Substantive human review by someone with editorial responsibility — not spell-checks or light read-throughs.

    Your next step: Build disclosure statements into your publishing templates now, before the deadline.

    Read the full guide →

    Cheers,

    Pranoti Kshirsagar
    Founder, The Science Talk

Hello hellooo,

"LinkedIn feels icky — what's the next platform scientists should be on?" 

An professor based in Netherlands asked me this question in one of our recent calls. 

It's a fair question. I've watched scientists migrate from Twitter to LinkedIn, and now LinkedIn is filling up with AI-generated noise, algorithm unpredictability, and the pressure to post constantly just to stay visible.

But here's what I actually think is happening — and why it changes everything about how you approach your online presence.

We are moving from platform-driven connections to people-driven ecosystems.

Right now, the platform decides who finds you. You go where the crowd is — LinkedIn, because everyone is on LinkedIn. The platform is the middleman between you and your audience.

That is starting to shift.

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I'm the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    The trend I'm seeing — and it's not unique to science, it's happening everywhere — is that people are increasingly choosing to follow people, not platforms. They find someone interesting, and they enter that person's universe directly: their newsletter, their website, their podcast, their community. Substack is the clearest current example of this, but it won't be the last. New individual-driven spaces will keep emerging.

    What this means for you: the platform you're on matters less than the foundation you build.

    If your entire visibility strategy depends on LinkedIn's algorithm, you're one platform shift away from starting over. But if you've built a platform-agnostic personal brand — one rooted in your voice, your audience, and your expertise — you move with the trends instead of being swept away by them.

    This is exactly the mindset we cover in the Personal Branding for Scientists workshop on 23 June.

    In 3 hours, across 6 modules, you'll walk away with:

    • A career goals framework that anchors everything you do online
    • A clear audience map so you know exactly who you're talking to
    • Your personal branding statement which is essentially your elevator pitch
    • A platform strategy built around your personality and comfort zone — not someone else's formula
    • Practical ways to use AI to make the whole thing easier and faster
    • And most importantly — your next 48-hour action plan so you leave with momentum, not just notes

    The mindset you'll learn is platform-agnostic. You learn it once, and you can apply it to whatever comes next — whether that's LinkedIn, a new emerging space, or your own corner of the internet.

    Because sustainable visibility isn't about being everywhere. It's about showing up in the right place, in a way that feels like you — not like a task on your to-do list.

    👉 Register for the 23 June workshop here

    Cheers,

    Pranoti Kshirsagar
    Founder, The Science Talk

Hello hellooo,

The ERC Advanced Grant 2026 is now open!

ERC Advanced Grant 2026

Call identifier: ERC-2026-AdG
Funding: Up to €2.5 million for 5 years (pro rata for shorter projects)
Additional funding: Up to €1 million for researchers already in the EU or an associated country; up to €2 million for researchers relocating from a non-associated third country
Additional funding now covers: Personnel costs (new for 2026)
Submission deadline: 27 August 2026, 17:00 Brussels time

What are the odds

35,258 proposals were evaluated for the ERC Advanced Grant scheme. 4,303 projects are funded. That's a 12% success rate.

Those are the odds you're working with. 

So when you sit down to write your proposal, every edge matters. 

And one of the most valuable edges is completely free — and most applicants never use it.

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I'm the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    The thing people skip

    The ERC publishes the titles and abstracts of every funded project. That means you can see exactly what kinds of research get funded, how successful applicants frame their work, and what language lands with ERC reviewers.

    This is not a small dataset.

    The ERC has evaluated over 143,846 proposals across all schemes and funded 18,587 projects. There is a lot to learn from.

    The problem? This information is scattered across different parts of the ERC website. Finding it, verifying it, and pulling it into something usable takes hours — if you know where to look at all.

    What I put together

    I spent time doing exactly that — tracking down, verifying, and compiling the most useful ERC resources into one place.

    The result is the ERC Advanced Grant 2026 Resource Kit: a handpicked, verified PDF with everything you need to study funded projects and write a stronger proposal.

    👉 Get the ERC Advanced Grant 2026 Resource Kit

    The ERC process is competitive, but you do not have to go in without preparation. The information is out there — and now it's in one place for you.

    Cheers,

    Pranoti Kshirsagar
    Founder, The Science Talk

    PS: If, apart from my email, you also need help strengthen impact strategy, I think you'll be happy about:

    1. Impact strategy for research proposals where I work with principal investigators who want professional science communication that matches the ambition and budget of their grant proposal. More details are on my website.

    2. ERC Starting Grant Resource Kit 47 official resources, organised in 11 sections including core webpages, ERC classes, compliance & AI guidance, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. You can access the kit here. 
    3. ERC Consolidator Grant Resource Kit 47 official resources, organised in 8 sections including core webpages, evaluation & panels, videos & webinars, results & examples, compliance & requirements, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. You can access the kit here.
    4. ERC Synergy Grant Resource Kit 44 official resources, organised in 10 sections including core webpages, ethics & compliance, videos & webinars, results & examples, compliance & requirements, AI guidance and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. You can access the kit here.
    The Science Talk

    Germany

Hello hellooo,

I often speak at conferences on various topics and I really love meeting people in person. The next few weeks are packed with 4 major events — and I'd love for you to be part of them.

This Friday - Quantum Day 2026, Stuttgart

🗓️ 12 June, 2:00–5:30pm · Stuttgart Media University · Free

I'll be giving a talk on quantum science communication and outreach, and joining the panel discussion afterwards. The theme this year is "Quantum and Beyond" — covering everything from post-quantum cryptography to quantum ethics. No prior knowledge needed. You can join in person or via livestream.
👉Register here


In two weeks - Personal Branding for Scientists in the Age of AI

🗓️ 23 June, 9:30am-12:30pm · Online · Paid
Registration closes 15 June
If you've been thinking about this one, now is the moment. 
👉Register here


Next month - EuroSTEMPeers 2026, Heidelberg

🗓️ 10-11 July · BioLabs Heidelberg · Paid 

On 10 July I'll be running a hands-on workshop on using AI for grant preparation and CV writing — practically and responsibly. The next day (11 July) I'll give a talk on the EU AI Act, which is genuinely worth knowing about before the August compliance deadline.
👉 Register here


Coming soon: Thriving PI Summit
🗓️ 29 June - 2 July · Online · Details and registration link dropping soon.

Lastly, if you're organising something — a workshop, a talk, a conference session — and think any of these topics would work for your group or institution, feel free to reach out. I'm happy to discuss what's possible, in person or online.

Hope to see some of you soon.

Cheers,

Pranoti Kshirsagar
Founder, The Science Talk

Hello hellooo,

Let me start with a number: €264 billion.

That's what European organisations — universities, research institutes, companies, public bodies — spend every year on cloud services provided by non-EU companies. Mostly Google, Microsoft, and AWS (Amazon).

Now, your first reaction might be: okay, but what does that have to do with me?

Fair. You didn't sign that contract. But your employer did.

But here's the thing — if you use Gmail, Microsoft 365, any HR software, any project management tool, basically any software at work — you are already sitting on top of that infrastructure. You're not responsible for it. You didn't choose it. But you're using it every day.

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    With AI entering the picture, this gets even more interesting.

    AI needs data. A lot of it. And that data needs to live somewhere — on a server, in a cloud. So as your employer starts integrating AI into workflows (or tries to), the demand for cloud capacity goes up. Which means the dependency on these non-EU providers deepens further.

    This is actually what made me go down this rabbit hole in the first place. I've been using AI tools in my work for the past three years, and at some point I started wondering: why is it so difficult for organisations to just adopt AI? Even when the potential is obvious? 

    Turns out, the answer isn't just about ethics or compliance or data security — though those matter too. It's also about the infrastructure. About what your employer's digital setup actually looks like underneath. And cloud dependency is a big piece of that puzzle.

    So in the latest episode of The Science Talk podcast, I go into exactly this — what the dependency looks like, where it sits, and why it's more layered than just "cloud services." There are multiple moving parts across cybersecurity and software that are worth understanding. Listen to the latest episode on Spotify 👇
      Listen on Spotify

      It won't change what software your employer buys. But it'll give you a much clearer picture of why AI adoption in European organisations is moving the way it is.

      Cheers,
      Pranoti Kshirsagar
      Founder, The Science Talk

        2. ERC Starting Grant Resource Kit 47 official resources, organised in 11 sections including core webpages, ERC classes, compliance & AI guidance, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. You can access the kit here. 
        3. ERC Consolidator Grant Resource Kit 47 official resources, organised in 8 sections including core webpages, evaluation & panels, videos & webinars, results & examples, compliance & requirements, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. You can access the kit here.
        4. ERC Advanced Grant Resource Kit 44 official resources, organised in 8 sections including core webpages, eligibility extensions, official documents, compliance requirements, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. You can access the kit here.

Communication and dissemination aren't the same thing — and treating them separately is what makes your research stand out. 

Communication builds your credibility over time. It's broad and ongoing — papers, conference talks, the general visibility you build just by doing good research and showing up in your field.

Dissemination works differently. It's the deliberate, targeted transfer of your research to specific audiences who can use it — think podcasts, videos, webinars, press releases.

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    Done well, dissemination is what opens the door to new collaborations, gets you on recruiter's radar, and helps you attract strong talent to your group.

    Both matter, and both are worth planning for — they just run on different timelines, different skills, and often different people executing them.

    Try this: Take one upcoming project or proposal.
    Ask yourself: who's my dissemination audience, and what's the one channel that actually reaches them?

    I've supported over 12 research proposals with total value well over  €32 million including Novo Nordisk Foundation, Klaus Tschira Foundation, Carlsberg Foundation, DFG, MSCA-PF, and ERC Synergy. 

    If you'd like help building dissemination into your next proposal, book a free 20-minute briefing call with me.

    Cheers,
    Pranoti Kshirsagar
    Founder, The Science Talk

      PS: If, apart from my email, you also need help strengthen impact strategy, I think you'll be happy about:

      1. Impact strategy for research proposals where I work with principal investigators who want professional science communication that matches the ambition and budget of their grant proposal. More details are on my website.

      2. ERC Starting Grant Resource Kit 47 official resources, organised in 11 sections including core webpages, ERC classes, compliance & AI guidance, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. Access ERC Starting Grant Kit.
      3. ERC Consolidator Grant Resource Kit 47 official resources, organised in 8 sections including core webpages, evaluation & panels, videos & webinars, results & examples, compliance & requirements, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. Access ERC Consolidator Grant Kit.
      4. ERC Advanced Grant Resource Kit 44 official resources, organised in 8 sections including core webpages, eligibility extensions, official documents, compliance requirements, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. Access ERC Advanced Grant Kit.

European Research Council (ERC) is running a free, one-day science communication training for grantees in November, and it's worth flagging if you're between year 2 and 4 of your project.

Travel and accommodation are covered. Around 40 grantees across all ERC schemes. Competitive, but a focused application makes a real difference.

WHO CAN APPLY
You're in year 2–4 of an ERC grant. Your host institution is in an EU Member State or Associated Country. Open across all schemes: Starting, Consolidator, Advanced, Synergy.

KEY DATES
Application deadline: 24 August 2026, 12:00 CEST
Notification: 10 September 2026
Training: 9 November 2026, Brussels (in-person)
Full details and application form: https://erc.europa.eu/news-events/events/science-communicati...

    A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
    My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
    My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

    HOW TO STAND OUT
    With 40 places and competitive selection, specificity beats length.

    • Name the audience you want to reach (journalists, policymakers, public) and why
    • Mention any comms activity already underway — lab blog, social media, anything
    • Link the training to a concrete near-term goal: upcoming dissemination deliverable, public engagement event, media opportunity

    WHY IT MATTERS

    Every ERC grant carries a dissemination and communication commitment. This gives you a direct, ERC-endorsed way to actually build those skills rather than just tick the box.

    The same skills — media engagement, policy framing, storytelling — are exactly what evaluators look for in the B2 impact section of future ERC proposals. Grantees who build a visible communication track record during their project walk into their next proposal with concrete evidence to cite, not just aspirational language. That's a real advantage.

    If November doesn't work for you, or you'd prefer one-to-one support building these skills into your next proposal, there's structured support available: https://thesciencetalk.com/proposal-writing-science-communic...

    I hope this was helpful🧡

    Cheers,
    Pranoti Kshirsagar
    Founder, The Science Talk

When creating content for science communication, you generally have two options:

  1. The Science Angle: You talk strictly about the research projects—focusing on scope, technical results, and future outlooks.
  2. The Human Angle: You focus on the scientist’s journey—their background, how they think, and the human story behind the discoveries.

At Under the Microscope*, we take the second, human angle. We put the scientist under the microscope, and through their personal and professional journey, we spotlight the incredible world of materials and nanoscience.


For those of you who are wondering what "Under the Microscope" is: Under the Microscope is an independently run self-financed podcast where we spotlight materials and nanoscience. As the host and executive producer I'm very happy and proud to share that we're in the 8th season and we've produced 300+ episodes featuring scientists from 40 countries.

A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

Inside the Latest Episode: Meet Dr. Anna Sandak

In our latest episode, this human-first approach brings us a fascinating conversation with Dr. Anna Sandak, Head of the Materials Group at the University of Primorska.

Rather than just listing research data, I sat down with Anna to explore:

  • From biology to building facades: How her background in biology inspired her to engineer living fungal coatings for architecture.
  • Living functionality: Why these coatings can self-heal scratches, absorb air pollutants, and use melanin to provide UV protection.
  • Grants & scale: The distinction between her ERC Consolidator grant (ARCHI-SKIN) and her commercialisation-focused EIC Pathfinder project (REMEDY).
  • "Living Tattoos": How high-resolution bio-printing combines artistic decoration with functional living microbial consortia on buildings.
  • Microgravity tests: Why her lab is sending fungal biofilms into space to test their resilience under extreme conditions.
  • Adoption: Her perspective on AI adoption for researchers ahead of the EU AI Act taking effect in August 2026.
    Read more about Anna Sandak episode

    📩 Feature Your Research

    Science is driven by the people behind it. If you would like to be featured on an upcoming episode of the Under the Microscope podcast—or want to discuss how we can support your project's science communication—simply reply to this email and let's start a conversation!

    Cheers,
    Pranoti Kshirsagar
    Founder, The Science Talk

Over the years, I've worked with and interviewed hundreds of scientists. And somewhere along the way, I started noticing a pattern - there are two types of scientists when it comes to communicating impact of their research.

Type 1 publishes in journals and goes to conferences. Everything beyond that is done half heartedly. Be it participating in public events liek open doors day or organising a summer school or posting on social media.

Type 2 does all of the above too. But with intention and a clear plan. Because they really care about communicating the impact of their research beyond their collaborators. They want to nurture the next generation of scientist through their summer school.

A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

Now...no matter which type feels relatable to you today, I can help you with your proposal.

Because I've worked with both types of scientists and got exceptional results. Scientists I supported at proposal stage won €8 million research grant and others went on to win awards for exceptional science communication.

This is how I work:

  1. I listen to you. You tell me about your creative ideas when it comes to science communication. Be it a website, social media channel, podcast / webinar series, or anything else.
  2. I give you a reality check. I tell you what it actually takes to build/maintain a website, social media presence, create videos, infographics.
  3. Together we finalise the text that goes in impact/SciComm section of your proposal.

Yes, it is that simple.
Book 20-min call with Pranoti

You see, I've done this work: running webinar series, building and maintaining websites, managing social media accounts, and producing podcasts start to finish, press releases, engagement analysis. So it is easier for me to give you informed suggestions so that you don't end up under- or over-promising in your proposal.

I look forward to working with you. 🧡

Cheers,
Pranoti Kshirsagar
Founder, The Science Talk

    PS: If, apart from my email, you also need help strengthen impact strategy, I think you'll be happy about:

    1. Personal branding workshop on Aug 25 (online) where I teach you essential elements of building your personal brand in digital spaces in the age of AI. Register for Personal Branding Workshop.

    2. Impact strategy for research proposals where I work with principal investigators who want professional science communication that matches the ambition and budget of their grant proposal. More details are on my website.
    Book 20-min call with Pranoti

    3. ERC Starting Grant Resource Kit 47 official resources, organised in 11 sections including core webpages, ERC classes, compliance & AI guidance, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. Access ERC Starting Grant Kit

    4. ERC Consolidator Grant Resource Kit 47 official resources, organised in 8 sections including core webpages, evaluation & panels, videos & webinars, results & examples, compliance & requirements, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. Access ERC Consolidator Grant Kit.

    5. ERC Advanced Grant Resource Kit 44 official resources, organised in 8 sections including core webpages, eligibility extensions, official documents, compliance requirements, and examples of winner grants - all in one pdf. Access ERC Advanced Grant Kit.

For scientists posting about their research on LinkedIn, Article 50 of the EU AI Act applies directly if they use AI to generate or manipulate their posts, unless they meet specific, strict exceptions.

IMPORTANT

If a scientist uses AI to generate or manipulate text for a LinkedIn post, it is legally considered "published text" because it is accessible to a large, indeterminate number of readers.

A special welcome to new joiners of this newsletter. 🤗
My name is Pranoti and I am the founder of The Science Talk.
My mission is to empower and enable scientists to share their stories in digital spaces with confidence and ease. 🧡

1. Text on "Matters of Public Interest" (Article 50(4))

  • Scientific developments with potentially important public implications are explicitly defined as matters of public interest.

  • If the purpose of the post is to inform the public on these scientific developments, the scientist must clearly disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. This includes using AI to write summaries or manipulate parts of academic papers.
Read "EU AI Act Article 50: Relevance & Obligations for Scientists"

2. Personal vs. Professional Activity

Under the Act, "deployer" obligations do not apply to natural persons using AI for purely personal, non-professional activities. However, a scientist posting about their professional research—especially if they are involved in a professional, academic, or freelance capacity, or if their post impacts public discourse—is considered to be conducting a professional activity. Thus, the scientist acts as a "deployer" and is subject to the rules.

This is exactly why my "Personal Branding for Scientists in the Age of AI" workshop on Aug 25 (in three weeks) includes a module dedicated to using AI tools for creating SciComm content. Register for Personal Branding for Scientists workshop Aug 25, 9:30am

Happy posting on LinkedIn🧡

Cheers,
Pranoti Kshirsagar
Founder, The Science Talk
